author: reek
body: dk-col-warn stays amber deliberately and is NOT re-themed: a warning painted in the brand palette is a warning that reads as decoration.

author: reek
body: The footer reserves one line height plus padding, because desk-shutdown paints its result inside the panel and a window sized to the body exactly would put that line on the desktop behind it.

author: reek
body: The chrome used `theme-terminal`, whose `pal-primary` is a generic terminal green shared with twenty-four consumers across twelve apps, so the sidebar buttons were the one part of the desktop that no palette change here could reach. This theme is built from the constants above instead, which keeps the re-theme inside this chapter: nothing else in the tree renders through it, and no other app's recorded frame moves.

author: reek
body: The brand label carries a minimum width. It has none by nature, and it read `CODEX` only because the compositor used to draw label text past the node's bounds; once text is cut to its own rectangle the label is exactly as wide as the layout made it, which was four characters.

author: reek
body: A pane hands back a WidgetNode and this puts it in the content panel, so the compositor lays the sidebar and taskbar out around it and the pane never learns the sidebar's width. GopScene and GopFiles predate this and each compute that offset themselves, which GopScene's own prose records as two files that "have to agree by hand".

author: reek
body: The right column opens with a spacer the height of the top bar, because `desk-topbar` paints over the laid-out tree afterwards. Without it the first row of any pane's content is drawn and then covered, which is what the calculator's display line did on its first capture. The sidebar is deliberately NOT given one: its brand label has always sat under the bar, and moving it is a change to the desktop's own frame rather than to this.

author: reek
body: Body text prefers the TrueType font read off the stick's own ESP; without one the CBF bitmap font stands in, and a status line names which is on the glass.

author: reek
body: Wrapping is by character count against the panel's inner width. The CBF glyph cell is 8 pixels wide at scale 1, which is exactly what gop-draw-text advances, so a line inside this count cannot overflow the bitmap path; the TrueType face is proportional and narrower at the same scale, so the same count is a safe bound for it too. A line that ran off the right edge was unreadable rather than ugly -- the text past the panel is simply not on the glass.

author: reek
body: The last space at or before the limit. Answering 0 means the run has no break in it, and the caller cuts at the limit instead -- a word longer than the panel is clipped by one line rather than looping forever.

author: reek
body: The blue bar is the dev console's own header row, which is where this shell's visual language came from: white on blue at the top edge, with the clock at the right end.

author: reek
body: The bounded tree comes back to the caller: it is the hit-test map that makes the sidebar buttons live.

author: reek
body: The clock sits at the right end of the blue top bar, repainting its own patch in the bar's colour so a redraw leaves no seam.

author: reek
body: The gate is the RTC second turning over, not the PIT tick cell.

author: reek
body: An unreadable second changes nothing and the loop asks again.

author: reek
body: The input state rides the clock, because the clock is the one thing on this desktop that repaints on its own. A keyboard that enumerates and never delivers is invisible in every other row -- the desk simply does not respond -- and on a machine with no serial port an unresponsive screen cannot be told from a hung one. `ev` is interrupt completions and `sc` is decoded scancodes; GopUsbKbd's own note enumerates what the pair distinguishes and which state no bed here can produce.

author: reek
body: The value column clears the longest label with a gap rather than by eye: "framebuffer" is 11 CBF cells, 88 pixels at scale 1, and a column at 88 puts the value hard against it with no space at all.

author: reek
body: The calculator pane. `GopCalc` owns the arithmetic and hands back a widget tree; this owns the loop and the chrome, so the compositor lays the pane out inside the content panel with the sidebar and taskbar around it.

author: reek
body: It repaints ONLY on a key that changed the state. `gcalc-key` answers whether anything moved, so a held or unrecognised key costs a poll and nothing else, and an idle calculator writes no pixels. That is the same promise the desktop's own loop makes and the reason there is no tick gate here: nothing in this pane changes on its own.

author: reek
body: The issue tracker's list view. The database is built ONCE on entry and held for the life of the pane: `tk-init-tracker-db` creates four tables AND SEEDS THEM -- its last line is `tk-seed-tracker s4` -- so calling the seeder again on its result inserts every issue twice, which is what the first capture of this pane showed: 28 rows, 14 issues, each listed with itself. Doing it per keystroke would also rebuild the catalog to answer a filter change. `ds` cells 32 and 40 hold the filter and the selected row, so the state survives leaving and re-entering the pane.

author: reek
body: The seeded store is the point of this rung rather than a limitation of it: the rows are inserted into a real catalog and queried back through the executor, so what reaches the glass has been through the data layer rather than around it.

author: reek
body: Up and down move the selection, `f` cycles the filter, and anything else costs a poll. Repainting only on a key that moved something keeps an idle pane silent, the same promise the calculator makes.

author: reek
body: The AssetForge screen. It is UNFINISHED and the pane says so on the glass rather than only in a backlog: Generate is a button nothing dispatches on, and the line under the preview names `works-backlog` WORKS-3. A dead control that admits it is a different thing from one that pretends.

author: reek
body: Painted once, then the loop waits for Esc. Nothing in this screen changes on its own, because nothing is generating.

author: reek
body: The self tail call keeps the loop constant-stack; the pet flag build keeps the watchdog quiet.

author: reek
body: Returning from an app repaints the whole desktop. The cursor hides BEFORE the repaint (restore then clear -- clearing alone bakes the old cursor pixels into the next saved patch wherever the repaint does not cover them) and is re-placed after.

author: reek
body: The desktop is the last thing standing on this machine, so Escape does NOT leave it. There is nothing behind it to return to and a stray keypress that blanks the screen reads as a crash. Shutdown is the way out, and it is a deliberate click rather than one key.

author: reek
body: The TrueType face comes off the boot medium through the same mount every storage screen uses; a stick without one leaves gf-ok False and the desk speaks CBF.

author: val
body: Three of these are the Seattle Seahawks brand colours exactly, and the rest are a ramp of College Navy so nothing on the desktop is a blue that belongs to nobody. The exact ones are the bar (College Navy 002244), the body text (Wolf Grey A5ACAF) and the hint line (Action Green 69BE28).

author: val
body: 524287 is 2^19 - 1, one bit per focus id at `dk-pedge-slots`, and it is a high LIMIT rather than a count because `gst-int-key` bounds a value. Widening the limit reads an older stored value unchanged, because every value the narrower limit admitted is still inside this one.

author: val
body: The controller reads the descriptor list and the samples by DMA after the call that starts the stream has returned, so both have to outlive the playback rather than the call. `desk-loop` restores the heap on every poll, so the click is rendered once at boot into a block the base mark cannot reach, and the click itself only writes registers.

author: val
body: Four rendered effects sit in the block at 16, eight bytes each (buffer, byte length); 48 holds a requested slot plus one, so zero is no request; 52 holds the focus id the last iteration saw. The focus tick is 40 ms at 600 Hz and four tenths of the click's volume: a switch between two windows is a quieter event than a press.

author: val
body: The CMOS RTC answers on ports 0x70/0x71 on every PC, virtual or real -- no VM convenience involved. Registers 0, 2, 4 are seconds, minutes, hours, BCD-encoded. `rtc-read` and the guarded `rtc-seconds` come from GopRtc, which waits out Update-In-Progress and reads twice: a raw seconds read from a fast poll loop lands in the update window constantly and answers garbage.

author: val
body: Port 0x403 IN is the codex-vm host rasterizer's present probe: it reads 1 under codex-vm, and bus-float on a real machine with no GPU driver.

author: val
body: Eight is the widget layer's character cell and 24 covers the padding either side. The sample is the WIDEST date the format can produce rather than today's, because a reservation that tracked the day would change width on the last day of a month.

author: val
body: It was the tick cell (28672, ~18 ticks per second) until 2026-08-04, when the ASUS TUF answered `pit=979` twice, 3405 seconds apart: the timer interrupt stops on that board at about 54 seconds and never resumes, while IRQ1 keeps delivering and the RTC keeps counting. A repaint gated on a dead counter never fires, so the clock froze and the Monitor pane below painted one frame for the life of the pane -- which reads as a hung desktop and was reported as one. The RTC is read off ports 0x70/0x71 with no interrupt, no PIC and no handler in the path; a machine that boots has one.

author: val
body: `28736` and `4072` are `stack-min-rsp-addr` and `ram-size-addr` from `codex/compiler/Emit/X86_64Boot.codex`. They are literals here because this chapter cannot cite the compiler, so they are hand-synced and will go stale silently if that file moves them.

author: val
body: THE SLACK IS A PAGE AND NOT THE MEASURED 200, and the reason is the failure mode. Undersizing a hole is not a refusal: `__deck-enter` arms a ceiling and an allocation past it TRAPS (`!EXC=06`, `PhaseAllocator.codex`), so a record that later grows by one field would turn a working desk into a fault. A page above the buffers is nothing against a hole of megabytes and removes that edge, and the arm is what keeps the measured figure honest.

author: val
body: 128 by 72 DEVICE pixels a slot: 36,864 bytes, times eighteen slots is 663,552 at boot, which is half a per cent of the flying image's 128 MB region. The alternative is a slot allocated on first minimise, and that cannot be done: a pointer parked in a `ds` cell must be allocated below the base mark or a pane exit hands the next visit freed heap.

author: val
body: A CELL READ BACK IS UNSIGNED, AND A WINDOW MAY NOW SIT AT A NEGATIVE X. `peek-32` zero-extends, so a `poke-32` of -362 reads back as 4294966934. `GopCalc` carries the same helper for the same reason and `GopAcpi` says it in words: a sign-extending load is what this platform does NOT do.

author: val
body: Six logical pixels, which is twelve device pixels at 1600. The grip has to be wider than the border it grabs or it is a pixel hunt, and narrower than the titlebar or a drag near the top corner becomes a resize.

author: val
body: BOTH THE COUNTER AND THE STORED START ARE MASKED TO 32 BITS. `peek-32` zero-extends and the HPET passes 2^32 in about five minutes at 14 MHz, so a full-width tick stored in a cell and read back is a different number. Masking both sides makes the subtraction wrap correctly, which is sound as long as the window is far shorter than the wrap period: one second against about 300.

author: val
body: THE COUNTER ONLY RUNS IF SOMETHING ENABLED IT, and until 2026-08-26 nothing here did. `hpet-start` sets the enable bit in the config register, and the only caller on the desk's side was `GopScene` building a scene -- so the HPET ran if you had opened the 3D pane and did not otherwise. `desk-run` starts it now. The first cut of this counter read a frozen counter, never closed a window, and therefore never painted at all, which is what made the missing start visible.

author: val
body: BIT 0 AND NOT THE WHOLE WORD, because a drag with a second button also down is still a drag.

author: val
body: 700 DEVICE PIXELS A SECOND, 24 LOGICAL PIXELS OF FOLLOW-THROUGH, AND 300 ms TO PRODUCE IT. The speed is a little under half a 1600-wide screen in a second: a throw passes it and a careful placement does not. The reach is scaled because it is a distance a hand makes rather than a count of pixels. The window is long enough that a hand still moving at the release has time to declare itself and short enough that a pointer moved later, for an unrelated reason, has already stopped counting.

author: val
body: Measured in the bed the repaint it skips is under 30 ms, which is not what Damian is seeing; the reason to cut it anyway is that this file records a desk paint as near a second ON METAL, where it is the whole gesture.

author: val
body: Tab cycles. It is Tab and not Alt-Tab because the desk tracks no modifier state: `kbd-take` answers a scancode and nothing accumulates a shift or an alt across calls, so an Alt-Tab today would be a claim the keyboard layer cannot support. The design's word for the feature is alt-tab and the key is Tab; that difference is written here rather than left for somebody to discover by pressing it.

author: val
body: NOT A SCANCODE, AND DELIBERATELY OUT OF THE RANGE OF ONE. A menu row answers the scancode the desk already dispatches for that pane, which is what keeps one table; Shutdown is not a pane and has no key. `desk-app-close-to` hands whatever a step answered back to `desk-dispatch` with `clicked` false, so a verdict that is not a real scancode rides the same road, falls past every `sc ==` in the table, and is caught at the bottom. Above 255 no PS/2 set can produce it, so this cannot be typed by accident at a power-off.

author: val
body: RTC registers 7, 8 and 9 are day of month, month and year, BCD like the time registers. The year register carries two digits, so the century is the caller's to supply and this assumes 2000. That reading is in `desk-wnd-tree` now, because the tree is what needs it.

author: val
body: `gsc-place` stores records allocated in the caller's frame, and the desk's per-iteration restore frees them, so every reader of the pane's placement places it first.

author: val
body: F12 writes the live frame to the boot stick as SHhhmmss.BMP and paints the verdict into the taskbar -- the telemetry channel that retires the camera rig. The whole capture is heap-bracketed: the 2-and-a-bit megabyte frame copy and the FAT image are reclaimed before the loop continues, after the verdict Text has been painted.

author: val
body: A SECOND CLICK ON THE SAME PILL WITHIN 400 ms PUTS THE WINDOW BACK AWAY, which is Damian's toggle. The first click of the pair has already run and raised the window, so the second is what makes the gesture a toggle rather than a second raise: click brings it up, click again puts it down. 400 ms is the interval every desktop uses for this and it is far enough below the flick's own 300 ms follow-through window to be a different gesture on a different control.

author: val
body: Both sides are masked to 32 bits for the reason `dk-rate-*` is: `peek-32` zero-extends and the HPET passes 2^32 in about five minutes, so the subtraction wraps correctly as long as the dwell is far shorter than the wrap period. 400 ms against about 300 s.

author: val
body: 16 and 14 are read off the sweep in `codex/test/apps/desk-leading-metrics`, which prints what the face answers at each ppem: 16 gives cap 11 and a 21 row cell, 14 gives cap 9 and 18 rows. Both sit in the range the reference does. The ppem is NOT multiplied by `ui-wscale`: it is already a device size, and doubling it at 1600 is exactly what made the type twice the size it should be. The larger of the two goes to the wider screen so the type does not shrink in proportion to the chrome around it.
